narrative: Based on the information provided in your application, the model has predicted a 51.8% probability that you would not pass the bar exam on your first attempt, which unfortunately led to the rejection of your admission. This prediction is based on a combination of your academic history and background, placing you just slightly over the threshold for a passing forecast. While your undergraduate GPA of 3.4 is actually higher than the 3.24 average of students who typically pass, your law school performance rankings—specifically being in the first and second deciles—are notably lower than the average successful student who usually ranks in the sixth decile. To help you understand this decision, we looked at "what if" scenarios, which are alternative versions of your profile that would have resulted in an admission offer. These scenarios identify the smallest changes needed to flip the model’s prediction from a failure to a pass. We generated ten of these alternative paths to see which factors were the most influential in your specific case. Interestingly, across all ten scenarios, the only factor that changed to trigger a "pass" prediction was your undergraduate GPA. In every single instance, the model indicated that if your undergraduate GPA had been 3.2 instead of 3.4, your application would have been accepted. This suggests that for a student with your specific law school decile rankings and lower-middle-income background, the model finds a 3.2 GPA more consistent with the profiles of those who successfully navigate the bar exam. Other factors, such as your LSAT score of 36 or your status as a full-time student, remained constant across all successful scenarios, meaning they were not the primary hurdles in this specific decision. While you cannot change your past grades, this analysis reveals that your current law school performance is the most significant area of concern compared to typical successful applicants. Students who pass the bar usually maintain much higher decile rankings throughout their first and third years than your current levels of 2.0 and 1.0. To improve your outlook, focusing on strategies to move from the bottom deciles toward the middle of your class would be the most effective way to align your profile with successful candidates. Even though the model's suggestion to have a lower undergraduate GPA seems counterintuitive, it highlights that your law school grades are currently the limiting factor relative to your earlier academic success. By narrowing the gap between your undergraduate potential and your law school rankings, you would significantly increase your probability of passing the exam. Ultimately, demonstrating a stronger upward trend in your law school deciles would likely override the model's current concerns about your predicted performance.
